findings:
No counterexample found and no proof (a proof would imply Lovasz's conjecture). No Lean file was written. Every graph tested satisfies the statement, each with a certificate (explicit Hamiltonian paths, re-validated, plus an exact integer solve).

REFORMULATION (checked against the Lean statement, no loophole found): averaging over Aut(G), the statement holds for G iff the vector of edge-orbit sizes lies in the cone spanned by the orbit-count vectors of Hamiltonian paths. A disproof needs orbit weights w with w.m <= 0 and w.c(P) > 0 for every Hamiltonian path P. Any partition into classes lying inside orbits gives a valid PASS.

RANGES VERIFIED (all pass, 0 unresolved):
- Orders 2-9: all 182 connected Cayley graphs (= all connected vertex-transitive graphs).
- Holt-Royle census, all connected vertex-transitive graphs of orders 10-39, 41, 43, 45, 47: 4,684,251 graphs.
- Orders 40, 42, 44, 46 restricted to degree <= 12: 1,268,890 graphs (degrees >= 13 not checked).
- Cubic vertex-transitive census (Potocnik-Spiga-Verret): all 50,113 graphs on <= 864 vertices, plus 2,423 graphs on 866-1280 vertices. Above 864 the complete orders are 866-878, 1182, 1262-1264; all graphs of girth <= 5 are done for orders 866-970 and 1250-1270. About 58,800 census graphs above 864 vertices remain unchecked (stopped for time; the machine was heavily shared).
- Exact enumeration of all Hamiltonian-path count vectors for the 290 cubic vertex-transitive graphs on <= 64 vertices.
The known range (circulants <= 14) is exceeded by a wide margin.

CROSS-CHECKS: an independent Python brute force agrees with the C checker on all graphs of orders 10-14; 319 certificates were re-verified by an independent Python verifier (0 bad).

THREE CANDIDATES THAT TURNED OUT TO PASS: the heuristics failed persistently on CVT[876,4], CVT[1264,187] and CVT[1152,3767]. Each was resolved by an explicit construction and then verified independently in Python (regular group of automorphisms, Hamiltonian paths, exact rational coefficients):
- CVT[876,4] = Cay(Z2 x (Z73:Z6); a, x), 146 hexagons: the alternating cycle (x a x^-1 a)^73 meets every hexagon once, giving a Hamiltonian cycle with 146 matching edges (the heuristic's minimum was 308, fair value 291.67).
- CVT[1264,187]: collapsing opposite blob vertices gives the generalized Petersen graph GP(316,157); almost any two suitable twice-crossed blobs give a Hamiltonian cycle with counts (476,318,470).
- CVT[1152,3767]: flag graph of a regular map of type {24,3} (192 vertices, 24 faces); "face cycles + bands" Hamiltonian cycles such as (431,470,250) put the fair point well inside the cone.
These constructions are now built into the checker (ftc_t.c, binary ftc17) as extra path generators.

PARTIAL LEMMAS:
1. Truncations T(B) (K_s blobs + perfect matching, B arc-transitive of valency s >= 3): every Hamiltonian path uses >= q-1 matching edges against a fair value of q - 1/s. So fairness of T(B) forces B to have a Hamiltonian path; for cubic B the two are equivalent. On truncations the statement is exactly Lovasz for arc-transitive graphs.
2. Among bounds from a single orbit or block system (cut bound, path-cover bound), truncations are the only tight case.
3. Cubic graphs with a 2-factor of 4-cycles: each odd "straight circuit" forces a twice-crossed blob, so t >= #odd/2 - 1, while fairness needs t <= (N+2)/3. Since #odd <= 2N/3, parity alone can never refute. The extreme case is the 2-arc graphs A(B), margin exactly 5/3 (exact data for B = K4, K3,3, Q3, Petersen).
4. Flag graphs of cubic maps with V vertices (new tight family): Hamiltonian cycles crossing every edge-quadrangle once use >= 2V "change-vertex" edges, spanning-tree "band" cycles use exactly 2V-2, and the fair value is 2V. Confirmed on exact data for the truncated cuboctahedron (CVT[48,26]).
5. Exact margins for cubic graphs <= 64 vertices: 2/3 for truncations, 5/3 for 2-arc graphs, larger otherwise. Heuristic slack exploration on ~13,000 dense graphs of orders 10-24 (order 24 partial) shows nothing tight except K_s-blob truncations (1 - 1/s), with no negative slack.

Conclusion: a counterexample of truncation type would refute Lovasz for arc-transitive graphs; none of the other mechanisms examined (parity, cuts, path covers) can separate the fair point, so a counterexample would need a new non-local obstruction. A Lean disproof is out of reach.

Files are in the folder given as file_path: checkers ft.c, ftc_t.c, exact.c; independent verifiers ref.py, verify_cert.py, hex/verify_cayley3.py, hex/transversal.py; logs in out/.
is_new: No resolution exists and none was obtained. The conjecture itself is new (posed 17 Nov 2026 by Luc Gillibert with GPT; lefttosolve.com); searches of arXiv, OEIS, Open Problem Garden, erdosproblems.com and MathOverflow found no paper mentioning it, no counterexample and no proof. It strengthens Lovasz's conjecture, which is still open: best results are cycles of length n^(1-o(1)) (arXiv 2609.38135, Li-Methuku) and arXiv 2606.09742 (Bucic-Christoph-Pokrovskiy-Steiner); arXiv 2407.00646 (Nakanishi) is an unverified claimed proof for odd order. On the tracker the only PR for this id is the closed statement PR #339 (Gillibert); there is no open PR (re-checked at the end). The computational verification (about 6 million vertex-transitive graphs, including the cubic census to 864 vertices) and the tight-family analysis (truncation equivalence with Lovasz for arc-transitive graphs, 2-arc graphs with margin 5/3, flag graphs of cubic maps) are to my knowledge unpublished, but they are partial evidence only and do not settle the problem.
